en.title: Adult Education: the whole course
en.short: What adult education covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What adult education is
sections.text: Adult education is the education of adults, and the study of how that education is planned, taught and evaluated. It includes literacy and numeracy, vocational skills, community development, continuing professional education, distance learning, workplace learning and education for marginalised groups. It is both a field of practice and an academic subject. It draws on psychology, sociology, philosophy, history, policy and research. It is not only the teaching of adults; it also covers needs assessment, curriculum, methods, materials, management, finance and evaluation. It overlaps with lifelong learning, non-formal education and community education, but each term has its own history and use.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text: Awards and lengths differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and the current regulations. In Nigeria, adult education is offered in universities, usually as a Bachelor of Education (B.Ed.) in Adult Education, and some colleges of education offer related routes through the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE). A full-time bachelor’s programme commonly runs for four years, but direct entry, part-time and sandwich routes differ. Master’s awards include the Master of Education (M.Ed.), and doctorates include the Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) and the Doctor of Education (EdD). In the United Kingdom and the United States, adult education is often studied within education, lifelong learning or extension studies, and named awards vary. Programmes usually combine foundation courses, core professional courses, electives, teaching practice or field experience, and a project or dissertation. Confirm the length, award and accreditation with your institution and the relevant national body.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course starts with the meaning and scope of adult education, then its history in the world and in Africa and Nigeria. It introduces philosophical foundations and the psychology of adult learning. Next come andragogy and pedagogy, especially Knowles and his critics, and the main theories of adult learning. Participation, barriers and learner support follow. Adult literacy concepts and measures close the introductory stage.

The core stage moves from needs assessment and programme planning to curriculum development. It covers teaching methods and techniques, instructional materials and resources, and adult literacy programmes and methods. Numeracy and functional skills come next. Then community development, extension education and rural development, distance and open learning, continuing professional education, and workplace learning and human resource development. The course also covers adult education for marginalised groups, guidance and counselling, assessment and evaluation, policy and financing, management and leadership, ethics and professionalism, and research methods.

The master’s stage adds critical theory, advanced research methods and the dissertation, and lifelong learning policy and the future of adult education.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Connect each idea to a real programme. Visit a literacy class, a community project or a workplace training session, and note how the session was planned, taught and evaluated. Keep a short journal of what you observe. This makes abstract terms such as needs assessment and learner support concrete.

Learn the key debates, not only the definitions. For andragogy, know Knowles’s assumptions and the main criticisms. For each theory, learn the author, the central claim and one limitation. Use examples from your own country, but name the country when you describe a policy or law.

Read official documents and current statistics with care. Figures on literacy, enrolment and funding change and differ by country. Always give the date and source, and check the latest official report before you rely on a number. Practise planning a short course: write aims, a needs assessment plan, a session plan and an evaluation plan.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
A common mistake is to treat adult education as only literacy or only the teaching of adults. It is a wider field of planning, management, policy and research. Another is to assume that all adults learn in the same way, or to apply child teaching methods without adaptation. Adults bring experience, responsibilities and sometimes distrust of schooling.

Students also confuse andragogy with a complete theory of adult learning. It is a set of assumptions and a teaching approach, and it has been criticised. Some present one country’s policy or funding model as universal. Others use old statistics without a date. In research, a common fault is to plan a programme without a needs assessment, or to evaluate only attendance and not learning. Always seek consent, protect privacy and report limits honestly.

keyPoints: Adult education is both a field of practice and an academic subject, covering literacy, community development, continuing education, distance learning and more.
Degrees and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and the current national regulations.
The course moves from concepts and history to core professional practice, then to critical and research-based study at master’s level.
Andragogy is a set of assumptions about adult learners, not a complete theory, and it has been criticised.
Connect theory to real programmes, learn the key debates, and give a date and source for every changing figure.
Avoid treating adult education as only literacy or assuming that all adults learn in the same way.

en.title: What Is Adult Education? Definitions, Terms and Scope
en.short: Defining adult education and separating it from adult learning, lifelong, continuing and non-formal education.

sections.heading: Defining the field
sections.text:
Adult education is the organised teaching of people who have taken on adult roles. It happens in colleges, workplaces, NGOs, government agencies and community groups, and it is a field of study too. A working definition: purposeful learning by adults, planned to meet their needs and usually voluntary.

It is not the same as adult learning. Adult learning is the process by which an adult person learns. Adult education is the organised activity, with a teacher or programme, that supports it.

sections.heading: Who counts as an adult?
sections.text:
Adulthood has several meanings. Biological adulthood is physical maturity, reached at puberty, and it varies. Psychological adulthood is self-direction, responsibility and a settled sense of self. Social adulthood means taking adult roles, such as worker, parent or citizen. Legal adulthood is the age a country sets for voting, contracts or marriage; it differs between countries and changes, so check the current law.

Programmes usually rely on the social and legal markers, and many accept anyone who has left formal schooling, whatever their age.

sections.heading: Terms that differ
sections.text: Lifelong learning covers learning from birth to old age, including children’s schooling. Continuing education usually means further study after an initial qualification, often in a profession. Non-formal education is organised learning outside the formal school system, usually without formal certification. Adult education often uses non-formal settings, but not always: a degree for mature students is formal.

sections.heading: Scope and myths
sections.text:
Scope runs from literacy and numeracy to vocational skills, health, civic and community education, distance study and workplace training.

Two myths are common. One is that adult education means only literacy or remedial schooling. The other is that adults cannot learn; they learn differently, not worse. Nor is it only for poor or uneducated people: graduates take courses too.

Case: a traders’ association in Kano, Nigeria, asks a facilitator to run evening bookkeeping classes. The classes are adult education; what the traders pick up from each other in the market is adult learning.

keyPoints: Adult education is organised learning for people in adult roles; adult learning is the learning process itself.
Lifelong learning spans all ages, continuing education follows an initial qualification, and non-formal education sits outside the formal school system.
Adulthood can be defined biologically, psychologically, socially and legally.
Legal ages of adulthood differ by country, so check the current law where you study.
The field covers literacy, vocational, health, civic, community, distance and workplace learning.
Adult education is not only literacy or remedial schooling, and adults can learn well.

en.title: History of Adult Education in the World
en.short: From self-help societies and folk schools to university extension, workers’ education and UNESCO policy.

sections.heading: Early self-help
sections.text: Mutual improvement societies were small, self-run groups where working people met to read, debate and learn useful skills. Mechanics’ institutes began in Britain in the early nineteenth century. They offered libraries, lectures and evening classes in science and technical subjects to artisans and factory workers. A typical institute might run classes in arithmetic and mechanics after the working day. These bodies showed that adults could organise education for themselves, outside schools and universities.

sections.heading: Folk schools and extension
sections.text: Danish folk high schools were residential schools for young adults, often from rural areas. They taught history, literature, citizenship and practical subjects, usually without examinations. N.F.S. Grundtvig, a Danish pastor and writer, inspired them, and the first opened at Rødding in 1844. They influenced adult education in many countries. University extension began in Britain in the later nineteenth century. Universities sent lecturers to towns and offered classes to people who did not attend full-time. It spread to the United States and elsewhere, linking universities with workers and communities.

sections.heading: Workers and policy
sections.text: Workers’ education grew with trade unions and labour movements. The Workers’ Educational Association, founded in Britain in 1903, and Ruskin College, founded in 1899, ran classes in economics, history and public speaking. The aim was often citizenship and social change, not only job skills. After 1945, UNESCO promoted adult education within lifelong learning, meaning learning across the whole of life. UNESCO’s CONFINTEA conferences, the International Conference on Adult Education, first held in 1949, set international policy. Later meetings included Hamburg (1997), Belém (2009) and Marrakech (2022).

sections.heading: Lessons of history
sections.text: Historians draw several lessons. Adult education has many roots: self-help, religion, social reform and vocational training. It often grows from social movements and democratic debate, not only economic need. Its purposes are contested, because liberal education and skills training can pull in different directions. Provision depends on the state, charities, unions and private bodies. Historians also warn against a single story. Adult learning took different forms in different countries, and access was often unequal.

keyPoints: Mutual improvement societies and mechanics’ institutes were early forms of organised adult education, often self-run or linked to work.
Danish folk high schools, inspired by Grundtvig, offered residential liberal education without examinations.
University extension carried university teaching to people outside campuses.
Workers’ education linked learning to citizenship and social change.
UNESCO’s CONFINTEA conferences, from 1949, shaped international adult education policy.
Historians stress that adult education has diverse roots and contested purposes, and access has often been unequal.

en.title: Adult Education in Africa and Nigeria
en.short: Colonial literacy, independence mass campaigns, university departments, and Nigerian and African professional bodies.

sections.heading: Colonial literacy work
sections.text: Colonial adult literacy in Africa was mostly small-scale. Mission schools taught reading and writing, often in local languages, for religious instruction. Colonial governments added basic literacy to welfare, health and agricultural extension work. Provision was uneven and selective, and it rarely aimed at mass literacy. Literacy here means the ability to read and write simple text. Adult education means organised learning for people beyond normal school age.

sections.heading: Independence campaigns
sections.text: After independence, governments saw adult education as a tool for development and citizenship. Tanzania under Julius Nyerere is the best-known case. From the late 1960s and early 1970s, mass literacy and adult education campaigns were tied to ujamaa, a policy of African socialism and self-reliance. They combined reading and writing with health, agriculture and civics. This is called functional literacy, where literacy is taught through useful tasks. Other African countries ran similar national campaigns, but results varied with funding, language and local organisation.

sections.heading: Universities and Nigeria
sections.text: Universities helped to professionalise the field. From the mid-twentieth century, many African universities created extra-mural studies units, which took courses to adults outside campus, and later departments of adult education. They trained teachers, researchers and administrators. In Nigeria, the National Commission for Mass Literacy, Adult and Non-Formal Education (NMEC) is the federal agency for literacy and non-formal education, meaning organised learning outside formal school. It works with state agencies and develops materials. The Nigerian National Council for Adult Education (NNCAE) is a professional association that promotes research, training and advocacy.

sections.heading: African networks
sections.text: Continental bodies link adult educators across countries. Examples have included the African Adult Education Association (AAEA) and the African Association for Literacy and Adult Education (AALAE). Such bodies have supported conferences, publications and advocacy. A small case shows the chain: a Nigerian state literacy office may use NMEC materials to train facilitators, a university department may evaluate the class, and NNCAE members may share the findings. Names and structures differ, so check current official sources.

keyPoints: Colonial literacy work was small-scale, often mission-led, and rarely aimed at mass literacy.
After independence, Tanzania under Julius Nyerere used mass literacy campaigns tied to ujamaa and functional literacy.
African universities created extra-mural units and adult education departments, helping to train practitioners and researchers.
Nigeria’s NMEC is the federal agency for mass literacy, adult and non-formal education.
NNCAE is Nigeria’s professional association for adult educators, and continental bodies have included AAEA and AALAE.
Provision and structures vary by country and change, so check current official sources.

en.title: Philosophical Foundations of Adult Education
en.short: Elias and Merriam’s five traditions and how each views aims, curriculum, teacher and learner.

sections.heading: A five-part map
sections.text:
Elias and Merriam set out five main philosophical orientations in adult education: liberal, progressive, behaviourist, humanistic, and radical or critical. Later editions of their book add analytical philosophy as a sixth. A philosophy of education is a set of beliefs about why we teach, what we teach, who leads, and who the learner is. They are lenses, not sealed boxes; programmes mix them.

Ask of each: What are its aims? What is the curriculum (what is taught)? What does the teacher do? What is the learner?

sections.heading: Liberal and progressive
sections.text:
Liberal adult education aims to develop the rational, cultured mind. Its curriculum is subject-centred: organised knowledge, great books, and disciplines. The teacher is an authority who transmits a tradition; the learner receives and exercises reason.

Progressive education aims at democratic living and problem solving. Its curriculum grows from learners’ experience and social issues. The teacher is a facilitator or guide; the learner is active and experience is central. In a class, a liberal teacher might use set texts; a progressive teacher might start from learners’ stories and a shared problem.

sections.heading: Behaviourist and humanistic
sections.text:
Behaviourism aims at observable behaviour change. Its curriculum is broken into sequenced objectives and small steps, with practice and reinforcement (consequences that strengthen behaviour). The teacher manages conditions and corrects responses; the learner responds to the environment.

Humanistic education aims at self-actualisation, meaning personal growth and fulfilment. Its curriculum is negotiated and whole-person, including feelings and life experience. The teacher is a facilitator and helper; the learner is self-directed and responsible. A safety course can be behaviourist when it drills correct procedures; a personal development group is humanistic when learners set their goals.

sections.heading: Radical and critical
sections.text:
Radical or critical adult education aims at social transformation and reducing oppression. Its curriculum is built around learners’ lived problems and critical analysis of power. The teacher is a co-learner who uses dialogue; the learner is an agent and critical thinker.

A community group might examine why market fees exclude women traders, then act. No tradition is complete; choose by context and values.

keyPoints: Elias and Merriam describe five main orientations: liberal, progressive, behaviourist, humanistic, and radical or critical.
Each orientation answers four questions: aims, curriculum, teacher role, and learner role.
Liberal education is subject-centred and aims at a rational, cultured mind.
Progressive education is experience- and problem-centred and aims at democratic living.
Behaviourism uses sequenced objectives and reinforcement to change observable behaviour.
Humanistic education aims at self-actualisation and self-direction, while radical or critical education aims at social transformation through dialogue and critique.

en.title: The Psychology of Adult Learning
en.short: How adult development, ageing, memory, senses, experience, self-concept, motivation and anxiety affect learning.

sections.heading: Development and ageing
sections.text: Development and ageing change learning capacity unevenly. Memory has short-term or working memory, where information is held while used, and long-term memory. Working memory and processing speed often slow with age, but long-term knowledge can remain strong. Intelligence is often described as fluid (speed and abstract reasoning) and crystallised (vocabulary and accumulated knowledge). Fluid ability may decline earlier; crystallised ability tends to stay stable or grow. Senses change too: presbyopia reduces near vision, and presbycusis reduces hearing high sounds. Good light, large clear print, quiet rooms and hearing support help. These are general patterns, not fixed limits for any person.

sections.heading: Experience and self-concept
sections.text: Experience is an adult’s richest resource. New learning sticks when it connects to what a person already knows, but experience can also carry habits and fixed ideas. Self-concept is the picture a person holds of themselves. Adults usually see themselves as responsible, self-directing people and may resist being treated as children. Respect, choice and shared control protect that self-concept.

sections.heading: Motivation and Houle
sections.text: Motivation is the force that starts and sustains learning. It can be intrinsic (interest, satisfaction) or extrinsic (promotion, certificate). Houle’s study of adult learners described three orientations: goal-oriented learners use education to reach a clear objective; activity-oriented learners join mainly for social contact or activity; learning-oriented learners study for its own sake. A learner may mix these. In a case, Amina, a 42-year-old nurse in Kano returning to study, may be goal-oriented (a promotion) and learning-oriented (curiosity).

sections.heading: Anxiety and teaching
sections.text: Anxiety about returning to study is common. Anxiety is worry and tension about a threat. It includes fear of failure, worry about maths or writing, and fear of looking foolish in class. Anxiety narrows attention and burdens working memory, so it can lower performance. Teachers can reduce it with a safe climate, clear expectations, small early tasks, formative feedback and chances to succeed. They should also recognise sensory and memory needs, build on experience, and offer support without lowering standards.

keyPoints: Adult ageing affects working memory, processing speed and the senses unevenly; crystallised knowledge often remains stable.
Experience supports new learning when teachers connect to it, but it can also entrench habits.
Adults’ self-concept as self-directing people calls for respect and choice.
Houle described goal, activity and learning orientations; learners can combine them.
Anxiety narrows attention and working memory, so safe, clear, step-by-step teaching helps.
Good light, clear print, quiet rooms and hearing support reduce sensory barriers.

en.title: Andragogy and Pedagogy: Knowles and His Critics
en.short: Knowles’ andragogical assumptions, their contrast with pedagogy, criticisms and a balanced view.

sections.heading: Two models
sections.text: Pedagogy is the art and science of teaching, often linked to teacher-directed instruction. Andragogy, a term Malcolm Knowles popularised, means the art and science of helping adults learn. Knowles set out assumptions about adult learners and contrasted them with assumptions he attributed to pedagogy. He later treated the two as a continuum rather than a strict age divide.

sections.heading: Knowles’ assumptions
sections.text:
Knowles’ andragogical assumptions:
Adults need to know why they are learning.
Their self-concept is self-directed.
Their experience is a resource.
Readiness is tied to social roles.
Orientation is problem-centred.
Motivation is mainly internal.

The pedagogical contrast is a dependent learner, experience of limited use, readiness set by schooling, subject-centred study and external motivation.

Implications for teaching include involving learners in planning, drawing on their experience, using real problems, and explaining relevance. The teacher becomes a facilitator, though direct instruction still has a place.

sections.heading: Criticisms
sections.text:
Critics raise several points. Evidence from research is weak: Knowles relied largely on experience and observation, and studies have not shown that all adults learn in these ways. The assumptions are not unique to adults; children can be self-directed in some tasks. Andragogy is a set of principles, not a full theory of learning.

The model also carries cultural bias. Its ideal of the independent, self-directing learner fits individualistic Western settings better than collectivist, or group-oriented, traditions, where learners may expect clear authority. It can overlook barriers such as class, gender, prior schooling and poverty.

sections.heading: Balanced use
sections.text: A balanced position treats andragogy as flexible principles, not a rule about age. In a literacy class in Kano, Amina, a trader, wants to read receipts. The teacher asks learners for their goals, uses market examples and group work. Some learners still expect the teacher to direct, so she blends short direct teaching with discussion. She assesses the group rather than assuming every adult is self-directed.

keyPoints: Pedagogy is often teacher-directed; andragogy is Knowles’ term for helping adults learn.
Knowles’ assumptions include self-direction, experience as a resource, readiness tied to social roles, problem-centred orientation and internal motivation.
The pedagogical contrast is a dependent learner, subject-centred study and external motivation.
Teaching implications include learner involvement, use of experience, real problems and explaining relevance.
Critics say research support is weak and the assumptions are not unique to adults.
Cultural bias and structural barriers mean andragogy should be used flexibly, not as a rule for all adults.

en.title: Theories of Adult Learning
en.short: Kolb, self-directed learning, Mezirow, communities of practice and Jarvis, with practice ideas.

sections.heading: Experience and reflection
sections.text: Kolb’s experiential learning cycle has four stages: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. A learner acts, reviews the action, forms an idea or rule, then tests it in a new situation. It is a model, not a fixed sequence. Jarvis’s learning process model begins when an experience does not fit the person’s biography, the store of past experience and knowledge. This disjuncture may prompt no learning, non-reflective learning, or reflective learning that changes knowledge, skills or attitudes. Practice: use real tasks, structured reflection and another attempt.

sections.heading: Self-directed learning
sections.text: Tough studied adults’ deliberate learning projects and found that many are planned by learners themselves. Knowles made self-direction central, with the teacher as facilitator of the learner’s own goals. Candy treated self-direction as both a process and a personal attribute, involving autonomy and control. It does not mean leaving adults alone: they may need help to set goals, find resources and review progress. Practice: use learning contracts, projects and negotiated plans.

sections.heading: Transformative learning
sections.text: Mezirow’s transformative learning explains change in meaning perspectives, the assumptions through which we interpret experience. It often starts with a disorienting dilemma, then critical reflection and discourse with others. Practice: create safe, respectful discussion; ask learners to examine assumptions; use journals and real problems. It is not just acquiring facts.

sections.heading: Communities and overlap
sections.text: Lave and Wenger’s communities of practice view learning as situated participation in a social group. Newcomers begin at the periphery and move towards fuller participation, called legitimate peripheral participation. Practice: apprenticeships, peer study groups and authentic projects. The theories overlap: all treat learning as active and experience-based, and reflection and social context matter. Case: Amina, a trader, joins a record-keeping class. A stock problem is a disjuncture (Jarvis); she reflects on assumptions about cash and credit (Mezirow); she plans a learning project (Tough); she tries new records and reviews them (Kolb); she learns with other traders (Lave and Wenger).

keyPoints: Kolb’s cycle moves through experience, reflection, conceptualisation and experimentation.
Tough and Knowles stress learners’ own planning; Candy adds autonomy and control.
Mezirow’s transformative learning uses critical reflection and discourse to change meaning perspectives.
Lave and Wenger see learning as legitimate peripheral participation in communities of practice.
Jarvis begins with a disjuncture between experience and biography, which may or may not lead to reflective learning.
All five theories treat adult learning as active, experience-based and shaped by social context.

en.title: Participation, Barriers and Learner Support
en.short: Who joins adult education, why, what stops them, and how support improves retention.

sections.heading: Who takes part and why
sections.text:
Participation means taking part in organised adult learning. Cyril Houle described three motives. Goal-oriented learners use education for a clear aim, such as a certificate or a better job. Activity-oriented learners join mainly for social contact or a shared activity. Learning-oriented learners seek knowledge for its own sake. People may have more than one.

Patricia Cross proposed a chain of response. A person first judges whether they can succeed. Attitudes to education, goals, and belief that study will meet those goals follow. Life transitions, such as a new job, can open or close the door. Opportunities and barriers come next, and information links the chain. Each link affects the next.

sections.heading: Barriers to participation
sections.text: Barriers are obstacles that reduce participation. Situational barriers come from a person’s life: cost, lack of time, transport, or caring duties. Institutional barriers come from the provider: fixed schedules, entry rules, distant campuses, or poor information. Dispositional barriers are internal: low confidence, fear of failure, or a belief that study is not for people like them. A learner often faces several at once.

sections.heading: Drop-out and retention
sections.text: Drop-out means leaving a course before completing it. Retention means keeping learners until they finish. Drop-out usually results from a mix of barriers and poor programme fit, not from one cause. Early warning signs include missed classes and falling work. Asking learners why they leave helps providers improve.

sections.heading: Learner support services
sections.text:
Support services help adults stay. Advice and information before enrolment help people choose the right course. Counselling can address academic worries, confidence, or personal problems. Childcare and transport support remove practical barriers. Flexible timetables, evening classes, and distance options suit working learners. Financial aid and learning support help.

Case: Aminu, a trader in Kano, wants a business certificate but cares for children and fears mathematics. Advice finds an evening course, childcare is arranged, and a tutor gives numeracy support. He stays and completes.

keyPoints: Houle’s typology describes goal-oriented, activity-oriented and learning-oriented motives.
Cross’s chain of response links self-evaluation, attitudes, goals, life transitions, opportunities and information.
Barriers are situational, institutional or dispositional, and learners often face several.
Drop-out is leaving before completion; retention depends on programme fit and early support.
Advice, counselling, childcare and flexible timetables are practical learner supports.
Support services should be planned, not added only after learners complain.

en.title: Adult Literacy: Concepts and Measures
en.short: Definitions of literacy and functional literacy, Street’s models, numeracy and how surveys measure literacy.

sections.heading: Defining literacy
sections.text:
Literacy is commonly defined as the ability to read and write a short simple statement on everyday life with understanding; UNESCO’s 1958 definition is close to this. Functional literacy goes further: a person uses reading, writing and arithmetic to function effectively in their group and community and to keep learning.

Definitions vary between countries and agencies and change over time, so check the source. A person may be literate in one language and not another.

sections.heading: Street’s two models
sections.text:
Brian Street (1984) contrasted two models. The autonomous model treats literacy as a neutral technical skill whose effects, such as better thinking or economic growth, follow from the skill itself. The ideological model says literacy is always learned and used inside social relationships and power. There are many literacies, not one.

Literacy as social practice follows this view: reading and writing happen in events shaped by culture, institutions and purpose. A market trader’s receipts and a school essay are different practices.

sections.heading: Numeracy and surveys
sections.text:
Numeracy is the ability to use numbers, measurement and quantitative reasoning in daily life; some call it quantitative literacy. Surveys measure literacy in two main ways. Self-report asks people whether they can read; direct assessment asks them to perform tasks. Self-report tends to overstate ability.

Example: a survey of 2,400 adults finds 1,560 can read a short sentence. The rate is 1,560 ÷ 2,400 = 0.65, or 65%. If 400 did not answer, the rate among the 2,000 respondents is 1,560 ÷ 2,000 = 78%. Always state the denominator.

sections.heading: Literacy and development
sections.text:
Schooling is a strong predictor of adult literacy, but many adults learned to read outside school, in literacy classes, religious settings or work. Literacy is linked with higher income and better health, yet the direction of cause is debated. Street’s critique warns against claiming that literacy alone produces development.

UNESCO treats literacy as a human right and part of lifelong learning. Rates differ by country and year; use current UNESCO Institute for Statistics data.

keyPoints: Literacy is the ability to read and write a short simple statement on everyday life with understanding, though definitions vary.
Functional literacy is the use of reading, writing and arithmetic to function effectively in one’s community and keep learning.
Street’s autonomous model treats literacy as a neutral skill; his ideological model sees it as shaped by social relationships and power.
Literacy as social practice means reading and writing are always embedded in context, institutions and purpose.
Numeracy is the use of numbers and quantitative reasoning in daily life, and surveys often measure it separately.
Self-report tends to overstate literacy, direct assessment is more accurate, and every literacy rate must state its denominator: rate = number literate ÷ total × 100.

en.title: Needs Assessment and Programme Planning
en.short: Bradshaw’s needs typology, data collection, and planning adult programmes from goals to review.

sections.heading: Bradshaw’s typology
sections.text: Bradshaw described four kinds of need. Normative need is judged by experts against a standard, such as a required literacy level. Felt need is what people perceive they need. Expressed need is felt need turned into action, such as enrolment. Comparative need is found by comparing similar groups: if a neighbouring district has a numeracy class and this one does not, a need may exist. Each kind has limits: experts may misread local life, felt need may be low when people lack information, expressed need depends on access and cost, and comparisons may use unsuitable groups. Use them together.

sections.heading: Collecting and prioritising
sections.text: Simple methods include questionnaires, interviews, focus groups, observation, community meetings, key informants and records such as enrolment and test results. Triangulation means checking a finding from more than one source. In an invented case in Kano State, Nigeria, a women’s group asks for tailoring. A survey also shows low numeracy, and traders report poor record-keeping. The planner ranks needs by how many people are affected, how serious the gap is, whether it can be addressed, cost and fairness.

sections.heading: Planning the programme
sections.text: A goal is a broad aim: improve women’s small-business skills. Objectives are specific and measurable: by the end of 12 weeks, 30 learners will keep simple sales records. Content follows objectives. Resources include people, rooms, materials and transport. The timetable must fit learners’ work and caring duties. Marketing uses radio, market associations and local languages. Learners should help set objectives, choose times and review sessions.

sections.heading: Budget and review
sections.text: An illustrative budget: venue 5,000 × 12 = 60,000; facilitator 8,000 × 12 = 96,000; materials 1,500 × 30 = 45,000. Total = 201,000. If each learner pays 500, income is 15,000, leaving a gap of 186,000 to fund. Review uses attendance, learner feedback, assessment and cost records; then revise the plan. Prices vary, so check local current costs.

keyPoints: Bradshaw’s four needs are normative, felt, expressed and comparative.
Use several data sources and triangulate before deciding priorities.
Prioritise by size, severity, feasibility, cost and fairness.
Goals are broad; objectives are specific and measurable.
Budget total = sum of item costs; gap = total cost − income.
Involve learners in planning and review the programme regularly.

en.title: Curriculum Development in Adult Education
en.short: Adult curriculum models, aims, content, sequencing, assessment, national adaptation and accreditation.

sections.heading: Models of adult curriculum
sections.text: Curriculum means the planned learning experiences of a course: its aims, content, sequence, methods and assessment. Four models are common. A subject-centred curriculum is built around academic subjects and their standards, as in adult secondary schooling. A learner-centred curriculum starts from learners’ goals, experience and needs, and may negotiate content. A problem-centred curriculum is organised around real tasks or issues, such as a community health problem, and may combine subjects. A competency-based curriculum states what a learner must be able to do, sets standards, and assesses by demonstration. Models can be mixed.

sections.heading: Aims and assessment
sections.text: Aims are broad statements of purpose; objectives are specific and measurable. Developers decide aims from needs assessment, national policy, community demands and the subject itself. Content is chosen for relevance, accuracy and feasibility. Sequencing usually moves from simple to complex, known to unknown, and concrete to abstract, with repeated practice. Assessment must match the aims: formative assessment guides learning; summative assessment judges achievement. Adult assessment often uses real tasks, portfolios and observation.

sections.heading: Adapting and integrating
sections.text: National curricula can be adapted, not ignored. Keep required standards and outcomes, then change examples, language, materials and timing to fit local learners. Integrate literacy and numeracy with skills by teaching them inside real tasks: reading safety signs, measuring cloth, calculating cost per plate, or writing an order. This is embedded literacy. It is more useful than separate drill when adults need the skill at once.

sections.heading: Accreditation and case
sections.text: Accreditation of non-formal learning gives official recognition to learning outside formal institutions. Providers map outcomes to a national qualifications framework, then use portfolios, challenge tests or observation. Recognition of prior learning, or RPL, credits what a learner already knows. Rules and bodies differ by country, so check the national authority. Case: a catering centre in Ibadan follows a national food safety standard but uses local market foods. Learners read labels, cost a plate, and are assessed by preparing a safe meal. An experienced cook may submit a portfolio for RPL.

keyPoints: Curriculum covers aims, content, sequence, methods and assessment.
Subject-centred, learner-centred, problem-centred and competency-based models can be combined.
Aims come from needs, policy and subject demands; assessment must match them.
Sequence from simple to complex and concrete to abstract, with repeated practice.
Adapt national curricula by keeping standards and changing local examples and materials.
Accredit non-formal learning by mapping outcomes and using portfolios, tests or RPL under national rules.

en.title: Teaching Methods and Techniques for Adults
en.short: Nine adult teaching methods, choosing among them, and facilitating discussion and mixed-ability groups.

sections.heading: Choosing methods
sections.text: A method is a planned way of organising learning. Choose by asking what the objective requires: knowledge, skill or changed attitude. Consider group size, available resources, time, and learners’ experience and confidence. A large group with little time may suit a lecture; a small group with a practical task may suit demonstration or project work. No method is best in every setting.

sections.heading: Nine methods
sections.text: A lecture is a talk by an expert; it is efficient for information but passive. Discussion is structured talk among learners; it builds reasoning. Demonstration shows a skill while learners watch and then practise. Role play asks learners to act a situation, such as a health worker advising a reluctant patient. Case study examines a real or invented problem in depth. Brainstorming collects many ideas quickly without judging them at first. Project work is an extended task with a product. Study circles are small self-directed reading and discussion groups. Peer teaching has learners explain to each other.

sections.heading: Facilitating
sections.text: For discussion, set a clear question, arrange seating so all can see each other, allow silence, and stop a few speakers from dominating. Summarise points and correct wrong statements. In mixed-ability groups, use varied tasks, pair stronger and weaker learners for peer teaching, and give extra time or simpler materials without lowering the goal. Watch for exclusion by gender, language or confidence.

sections.heading: A case
sections.text: In a literacy class in Ibadan, facilitator Mrs Adeyemi wants learners to read a medicine label. She demonstrates with a label, then pairs learners to role play asking a pharmacist. She uses a short case of a child given the wrong dose, then a brainstorm on prevention. The project is a poster. She chooses these methods because the objective is practical, the group is small, and time is short.

keyPoints: Choose a method by objectives, group size, resources, time and learner experience.
Lecture is efficient for information but passive; discussion builds reasoning.
Demonstration, role play and project work suit skill and attitude goals.
Brainstorming gathers ideas before judgement; case study and study circles deepen analysis.
Facilitate discussion with a clear question, fair turn-taking and summary.
In mixed-ability groups, vary tasks and use peer teaching without lowering the goal.

en.title: Instructional Materials and Resources
en.short: How to choose, design, test and evaluate printed, audio, visual, real-object and local materials for adults.

sections.heading: Types of materials
sections.text: Instructional materials are resources that support learning. Printed materials include handouts, workbooks, posters and flip charts. Audio materials carry sound only, such as radio, recordings and phone audio. Visual materials carry images without sound, such as diagrams and photographs. Real-object materials, or realia, are actual tools, seeds or machines used in demonstration. Locally made materials are produced near learners, often from cheap local materials and local examples. The groups overlap: a poster is printed and visual; a video is audio-visual.

sections.heading: Choosing and designing
sections.text:
Select materials by asking whether they match the objective, learners’ reading level, language, experience and setting. Check accuracy, clarity, cultural fit and accessibility, including low literacy and disability. Consider cost, durability and easy replacement. Adults have experience and little time, so avoid childish tone and give practical examples.

Design with one main idea per item, large clear images, short sentences and local names. Use learners’ language where possible and leave space for discussion and action. Case: a health class in Kano uses a locally drawn poster on oral rehydration, plus a real cup and spoon. The poster is printed and visual; the cup and spoon are realia.

sections.heading: Low-cost, radio, phones
sections.text: Low-cost production means using what is available: hand-drawn posters, chalkboards, recycled card, local artists and learner-made materials. Keep designs simple so they can be copied and repaired. Radio reaches distant learners and can carry drama, discussion and phone-in programmes. Mobile phones support audio lessons, text reminders, pictures and short videos. Check network coverage, power supply and data cost first. Do not assume every learner has a smartphone.

sections.heading: Testing and evaluating
sections.text: Test with a small group like intended learners before full use. Ask them to explain the message, use the item and say what is unclear. Check reading level, image clarity and cultural fit. Revise and test again. Evaluate by watching participation, asking for feedback and checking whether learning changed. Record cost, breakages and time. A material that is accurate but unused has failed.

keyPoints: Printed, audio, visual and real-object materials are categories that often overlap.
Locally made materials use nearby people, language and cheap materials, but may wear out faster.
Choose materials that match the objective, learners’ language and experience, and the setting.
Check accuracy, clarity, cultural fit, accessibility, cost and durability.
Low-cost production, radio and mobile phones widen access, but check power, network and data cost.
Test materials with a small group, revise them, and evaluate whether learning changed.

en.title: Adult Literacy Programmes and Teaching Methods
en.short: Comparing five literacy methods, plus class planning, primers and assessment.

sections.heading: Comparing methods
sections.text:
Phonics teaches letter-sound links and blending, helping learners decode new words; English spelling is irregular, so phonics needs plenty of meaningful practice. The whole-word or look-and-say method teaches common words by sight, often with pictures. It gives quick success but little help with decoding new words.

The language experience approach uses the learner’s own speech: the learner dictates a story, the teacher writes it, and that text becomes reading material. It builds confidence and meaning, but needs a teacher who writes the learner’s language well. Many classes combine methods.

sections.heading: Laubach and Freire
sections.text:
Frank Laubach’s method is structured and phonics-based. A key word and picture lead to syllables and letters, practised in charts. 'Each One Teach One' means a new reader teaches another. It is cheap and reproducible, but can be teacher-centred.

Paulo Freire’s approach uses generative themes and words from learners’ lives, such as water or wages. A culture circle discusses a picture, then breaks a key word into syllables. Literacy links to dialogue and action. It is participatory but needs skilled facilitation and may give less decoding practice. A programme can combine Freire’s themes with Laubach’s structure.

sections.heading: Planning and primers
sections.text:
Plan from a needs assessment: who are the learners, what language, what purposes, when and where they can meet. Set small, practical objectives. Use local words, signs and stories. Arrange seats in a circle for talk, and keep sessions short.

A primer is a graded reading book for beginners. Build it in steps: picture and key word, letter-sound practice, a short sentence, then review. Field-test it with a few learners. For example, a market class in Kano might start with price words and a simple receipt.

sections.heading: Assessing progress
sections.text: Assess at entry, during and at the end. Use oral reading, word recognition, dictation, a short writing sample and comprehension questions. Keep a simple portfolio and record each learner’s gains. Assessment should match the method taught and should encourage, not shame, adults.

keyPoints: Phonics builds decoding through letter-sound links; whole-word builds quick sight vocabulary.
The language experience approach turns the learner’s dictated speech into reading text.
Laubach’s method is structured and phonics-based, with 'Each One Teach One'.
Freire’s generative themes link literacy to dialogue and action on learners’ problems.
Plan from a needs assessment, use local words, and build graded primers tested with learners.
Assess with oral reading, dictation, writing samples and portfolios, and use results to adjust teaching.

en.title: Numeracy and Functional Skills
en.short: Definitions, everyday maths teaching, integration with literacy and work, and assessing functional competence.

sections.heading: Defining the terms
sections.text:
Numeracy is the ability to use mathematical knowledge, reasoning and tools to solve problems in real situations. It includes number sense, measurement, money, data and checking whether an answer is reasonable. Functional skills are the practical skills needed for everyday tasks at home, work and in the community, usually literacy, numeracy and digital skills. In England, functional skills also names a set of qualifications; check current official rules.

Adults need them to manage wages and budgets, follow instructions, measure materials, understand health information, help children and take part in public life.

sections.heading: Teaching everyday maths
sections.text:
Teach from real tasks, then draw out the mathematics. Use shopping, payslips and sharing for number; cooking, tailoring and building for measurement; budgets and price comparison for money. Follow a cycle: understand, choose a method, work out, check.

Worked example: a room is 4.5 m by 3.2 m. Area = 4.5 × 3.2 = 14.4 m². A 0.3 m square tile covers 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09 m². Tiles = 14.4 ÷ 0.09 = 160. Add 10%: 160 × 0.10 = 16, so buy 176 tiles.

sections.heading: Linking literacy and work
sections.text: Integrate numeracy with literacy by reading labels, forms, bills and word problems, and by asking learners to explain their reasoning. In vocational training, teach the maths of the trade: ratios for mixing, areas for materials, stock records, unit prices and simple costing. Use learners’ own work problems, keep language plain, teach maths vocabulary, and move from concrete objects to pictures and symbols.

sections.heading: Assessing functional competence
sections.text: Assess what learners can do in realistic tasks, not only what they can recall. Use performance tasks, observation checklists, portfolios and short projects. State criteria clearly: chooses the right operation, shows working, uses units correctly, checks the answer and explains it. Give feedback and let learners repeat a similar task. Paper tests can support this but should not be the only evidence. Functional competence means transferring skills to a new situation.

keyPoints: Numeracy is the use of mathematics to solve real problems; functional skills are the practical skills needed for daily life and work.
Adults need numeracy for money, measurement, health information, work and participation.
Teach from real tasks and use a cycle: understand, plan, solve, check.
Area = length × width; percentage = part ÷ whole × 100; total cost = unit price × quantity.
In vocational and literacy teaching, connect maths to labels, forms, trade tasks and learners’ own problems.
Assess functional competence with realistic performance tasks and clear criteria, not only paper tests.

en.title: Community Development and Adult Education
en.short: Community development, needs assessment, participation, Freire’s conscientisation and project evaluation.

sections.heading: Facilitator and animator
sections.text:
Community development is a process in which people in a place or shared group identify what matters, plan together and act to improve their conditions. It is not a service delivered to passive recipients.

The adult educator supports learning within that process. As a facilitator, the educator helps people discuss, decide and learn from action instead of supplying answers. As an animator, the educator mobilises people, builds confidence and keeps participation alive. The role is sometimes called animation in Francophone community work. An outsider needs listening and humility.

sections.heading: Needs and participation
sections.text:
Community needs assessment is a systematic way to learn what people need and what they already have. It should be participatory: use public meetings, focus groups, community mapping and ranking of problems. Ask who is absent, including women, young people, disabled people and poor households. Participatory methods treat local knowledge as evidence.

In a fictional case, residents of a ward in Ogun State, Nigeria, map water points and rank repairs. The educator records the discussion, helps the group check facts and asks what they can do before seeking outside help.

sections.heading: Conscientisation and evaluation
sections.text:
Conscientisation, in Paulo Freire’s sense, is the growth of critical awareness: people see the causes of their situation and act on them. It is more than information. Freire, a Brazilian educator, described dialogue and problem-posing education in Pedagogy of the Oppressed. Community associations, such as cooperatives, market women’s groups, youth clubs and faith groups, hold trust and resources. Work with them respectfully, strengthen their planning and records, and avoid creating a rival group.

Evaluation asks what changed. Agree indicators, meaning checkable signs, at the start. Distinguish outputs, such as a training session held, from outcomes, such as cleaner water. Use a baseline, the situation before, then monitor and review with the community. Ask who benefited and who was left out, and feed lessons into the next plan.

keyPoints: Community development is participatory action by community members, not a service delivered to them.
The adult educator works as facilitator and animator, supporting local decisions and confidence.
Needs assessment should include absent groups and treat local knowledge as evidence.
Conscientisation means critical awareness of causes plus action, in Freire’s sense.
Community associations should be strengthened, not replaced by rival groups.
Evaluation compares agreed indicators with a baseline and distinguishes outputs from outcomes.

en.title: Extension Education and Rural Development
en.short: Agricultural extension, rural development education, farmer field schools, diffusion and low-literacy adaptation.

sections.heading: Extension and rural development
sections.text:
Agricultural extension is non-formal education and advice that helps farming households improve production, income and well-being. It starts from farmers’ problems and involves them in testing solutions. Rural development education is wider: it builds knowledge and skills for planning and acting on local development, including health, water, markets and institutions.

Both treat rural people as adult learners and decision-makers. They use group meetings, field days, visits and practical training. The aim is change farmers can sustain, not a one-off message.

sections.heading: Workers and field schools
sections.text:
The extension worker is a facilitator, trainer and link between farmers, researchers, government and markets. The role includes listening, diagnosing problems, organising learning and helping groups demand services.

A farmer field school is a group learning approach, often season-long, held in a field. Farmers observe crops, compare plots, discuss and decide. Farmer field schools became known through integrated pest management work in Indonesia in the late 1980s, supported by FAO. A demonstration plot is a small field where a new practice is shown beside the usual practice, so people can see and discuss the difference.

sections.heading: Diffusion, literacy and cooperatives
sections.text:
Diffusion of innovations studies how new ideas spread. Adoption is faster when an innovation has clear relative advantage, fits local values, is simple, can be tried on a small scale, and gives visible results.

For low-literacy audiences, use local language, pictures, drama, radio and hands-on practice, and check understanding by asking learners to explain or show a step. Link extension with functional literacy classes that use farming examples, and with cooperatives, which are member-owned groups that buy, sell, save or process together. Extension can train members in records, governance and bargaining.

Case: an extension worker helps Amina’s group in Kano State, Nigeria, compare an improved maize practice with the local practice on two small plots. Farmers visit, ask questions and record what they see. Those who want to try it do so on a small area first, then discuss results with the group.

keyPoints: Agricultural extension is non-formal education and advice for farming households; rural development education is wider.
An extension worker facilitates learning and links farmers with researchers, services and markets.
Farmer field schools are season-long group learning in fields; demonstration plots compare a new practice with the usual one.
Diffusion of innovations explains how new ideas spread; relative advantage, compatibility, simplicity, trialability and visible results speed adoption.
Low-literacy audiences need oral, visual, local-language and hands-on methods, not written-only materials.
Link extension with functional literacy and cooperatives so farmers can read, organise, keep records and bargain.

en.title: Distance and Open Learning
en.short: Definitions, history, key concepts, delivery media, quality assurance and access in distance and open learning.

sections.heading: Definitions and history
sections.text:
Distance education is planned teaching and learning where teacher and learner are separated in place or time, linked by materials and communication. Open learning is a policy or philosophy that removes barriers to study: entry requirements, fixed schedules and campus attendance. They overlap but differ: distance courses can be closed, and open learning can be face to face.

Correspondence education using posted print began in the nineteenth century. From the 1960s open universities combined distance methods with open entry, and online delivery grew from the 1990s.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.text:
Independent study means learners work through prepared materials at their own pace, taking responsibility for reading, practice and deadlines. It does not mean isolation: learner support supplies tutors, feedback, advice, library access and peer contact.

Open entry admits students without academic prerequisites, sometimes with preparatory courses or diagnostic assessment. These ideas shape course design: clear objectives, self-check activities and contact.

sections.heading: Delivery modes
sections.text:
Print remains central where electricity or internet is unreliable; it is portable and cheap to distribute, but slow to update. Radio reaches scattered learners at low cost and suits discussion, health and farming topics, but is one-way unless combined with phones or study centres. Online delivery allows video, forums and quick updates, but requires devices, data, electricity and digital skills.

Case: Amina, a trader in Kano, studies a diploma through an open university. Printed modules arrive by post, a weekly radio lesson explains business records, and a tutor answers questions by phone.

sections.heading: Quality and access
sections.text:
Quality assurance checks that distance provision is credible: recognised accreditation, reviewed materials, trained tutors, fair assessment, secure exams and usable learner support. It should compare outcomes with campus programmes, not merely inputs.

Open universities widen adult access by scaling up, lowering entry barriers and allowing study alongside work and family. They can reach rural learners and women with restricted mobility. Yet access is not equity: fees, connectivity, disability and digital literacy still exclude people, and qualifications need employer and regulator recognition.

keyPoints: Distance education separates teacher and learner in place or time and links them through materials and communication.
Open learning removes barriers such as entry requirements, fixed schedules and campus attendance; it is not identical to distance education.
Independent study gives learners responsibility for pace and practice, while learner support provides tutors, feedback and contact.
Open entry admits learners without usual prerequisites, often with preparatory or diagnostic help.
Print, radio and online delivery each have strengths and limits, so programmes usually mix media.
Quality assurance and recognition matter, and open universities widen access but do not by themselves remove cost, connectivity and disability barriers.

en.title: Continuing Professional Education
en.short: CPE, mandatory CPD, professional body rules, needs assessment, accreditation and learner autonomy.

sections.heading: CPE and CPD
sections.text:
Continuing professional education (CPE) is learning after initial qualification that keeps a professional competent. Continuing professional development (CPD) is the wider process of that learning across a whole career, including courses, conferences, reading, mentoring and reflective practice. Reflective practice means thinking critically about your own work to improve it.

CPE is often formal; CPD can be formal or informal. It matters because knowledge and rules change, and the public expects safe practice.

sections.heading: Rules and requirements
sections.text:
Professional bodies, regulators and employers set requirements. A body may require a number of CPD hours or points each year, a record, and an annual declaration.

Some professions make CPD mandatory for licence renewal; others expect it but do not police it. Rules differ by country and profession, so check the current handbook of your own body. Mandatory CPD is sometimes called compulsory CPD or mandatory continuing professional education.

sections.heading: Assessing needs
sections.text:
Needs assessment for professionals compares what is required with what the person can do now. It uses self-assessment, appraisals, standards, audit data and peer feedback. The result is a learning plan with priorities.

For example, suppose a body requires 30 CPD hours a year, with at least 10 in technical subjects. A learner records 12 technical, 8 ethics and 6 management hours: 12 + 8 + 6 = 26, so 4 hours are still needed, and the technical minimum is met.

sections.heading: Accreditation and autonomy
sections.text:
Accreditation is approval of a course by a professional body or quality agency. It checks aims, content, teachers, assessment and resources, and may award CPD points.

Accreditation helps learners choose trustworthy courses, but it can narrow what counts as learning. The tension is between employer needs, which stress immediate job skills and compliance, and learner autonomy, which stresses personal goals and critical judgement. Good CPD systems allow negotiated plans, reflection and a mix of formal and informal learning.

keyPoints: CPE is post-qualification learning; CPD is the wider process of formal and informal professional learning across a career.
Professional bodies and regulators set CPD requirements, but rules vary by country and profession.
Mandatory CPD links learning to licence or membership renewal; voluntary CPD relies on professional commitment.
Needs assessment compares required standards with current competence and produces a learning plan.
Accreditation is quality approval of a course by a professional or quality body.
Employer needs and learner autonomy can conflict; negotiated plans and reflection help balance them.

en.title: Workplace Learning and Human Resource Development
en.short: Workplace and informal learning, HRD, training needs analysis, mentoring, apprenticeships and who pays.

sections.heading: Workplace learning
sections.text: Workplace learning is learning that happens through work. It may be planned, as in induction, or unplanned, as when a worker solves a problem with a colleague. Informal learning is the unplanned part: observing, asking, trying and reflecting. Much of it is tacit, meaning hard to write down. Human resource development (HRD) is the organised learning and development an organisation provides to improve individual capability and performance. HRD includes training, career development and organisational development, but is narrower than adult education.

sections.heading: Training needs analysis
sections.text: Training needs analysis (TNA) is a systematic way to decide what learning is needed. It compares required with present performance and asks why the gap exists. It covers the organisation, the task and the individual. Methods include observation, interviews, records and surveys. The output is learning objectives and priorities. A Lagos bakery, for example, finds that new staff mislabel orders. A TNA may show the cause is unclear written instructions, not lack of skill. The answer may be a clearer checklist and coaching, not a full course.

sections.heading: Mentoring and apprenticeships
sections.text: Mentoring pairs a less experienced person with a more experienced one for advice, support and role modelling. It is developmental, not formal assessment. An apprenticeship combines work with off-the-job learning and leads to a recognised skill or qualification. Its rules, pay and length vary by country, so check the national system. A learning organisation continuously improves by encouraging learning, sharing knowledge and reviewing results. Peter Senge popularised the term. Learning becomes daily work, not a one-off event.

sections.heading: Who should pay
sections.text: Who should pay for work-related learning is disputed. Employers gain from productivity but may underinvest if trained staff leave. Workers gain from skills and wages but may not afford fees. Society gains from growth and safer services. Arguments support employer funding, public funding, or shared models such as training levies, where employers pay into a training fund, and tax incentives. Policy differs by country, so check current official rules. The fairest answer depends on who gains and how portable the skill is.

keyPoints: Workplace learning includes planned training and unplanned learning from work itself.
Informal learning is often tacit and hard to document.
HRD is organised learning and development for individual and organisational performance.
Training needs analysis compares required and present performance before choosing a solution.
Mentoring is developmental support; apprenticeships combine work and off-the-job learning under national rules.
Who pays for work-related learning is debated; policy varies by country, so check current official rules.

en.title: Adult Education for Marginalised Learners
en.short: Barriers facing excluded groups, inclusive design, gender-responsive literacy, disability access and recruitment.

sections.heading: Barriers
sections.text: Marginalised learners are groups pushed to the edge of education by social, economic or physical barriers. Women often face time poverty from unpaid care, early marriage, unsafe travel and male-dominated classes. Rural people face long distances, transport costs, seasonal work and few trained facilitators. Persons with disabilities meet steps, no sign language, print-only materials and stigma. Older adults may have poor sight or hearing, ill health and low confidence. Prisoners face security rules, short sentences and stigma. Out-of-school youth have interrupted schooling, child labour or displacement and need flexible, accelerated routes. Barriers overlap: a rural woman with a disability may face distance, cost and inaccessible venues at once.

sections.heading: Inclusive design
sections.text:
Inclusive programme design builds the course around excluded learners from the start. Use local languages, flexible times and venues, free or low-cost enrolment, childcare and transport support. Train facilitators in participatory methods and respect. Involve the target group in planning and monitoring, and record participation by sex, age, disability and location so gaps show.

Gender-responsive literacy means content and methods respond to women’s lives. It may include health, rights, savings and farming, female facilitators, women-only circles, and times that fit care work. Disability access means universal design, such as step-free rooms, captions, sign language, braille or large print, plus reasonable accommodation, an individual adjustment such as extra time or a support worker.

sections.heading: Recruitment and examples
sections.text:
Targeted recruitment reaches people where they are. Use radio, markets, religious and traditional leaders, women’s groups, disabled persons organisations, prisons and youth centres. Remove small costs that exclude.

In Africa, REFLECT is a participatory literacy approach used in several countries, including Uganda and Ghana. It links reading and writing to local action, such as water or health problems. Uganda’s Functional Adult Literacy programme uses community classes and local language materials. A hypothetical case: in a rural Ghanaian district, a women’s circle meets after harvest, with a female facilitator and childcare. The group reads clinic notices and plans a safe-water request. A ramp and sign-language interpreter let two deaf women join. Design, access and recruitment work together.

keyPoints: Marginalised groups face economic, social, physical and institutional barriers that often overlap.
Women need gender-responsive literacy: relevant content, female facilitators, safe venues and times that fit care work.
Rural learners need local languages, flexible schedules and reduced distance and cost.
Disability access means universal design plus reasonable accommodation, not separate classes only.
Targeted recruitment uses trusted networks and removes small costs that exclude.
Older adults, prisoners and out-of-school youth need respectful pace, secure settings and flexible or accelerated routes.

en.title: Guidance and Counselling for Adult Learners
en.short: Educational guidance, counselling, prior learning assessment, study help, ethics and referral.

sections.heading: Guidance and counselling
sections.text: Educational guidance helps an adult learner choose courses, entry routes and progression. It is mainly information and advice; the learner decides. Counselling is a helping conversation about feelings, confidence or personal difficulties that affect study. It is not discipline or academic assessment. Guidance may be brief and informal, while counselling needs privacy and time. Both respect the learner’s choice.

sections.heading: Prior learning
sections.text: Assessment of prior learning checks what a learner already knows from work, volunteering or earlier study. Recognition of prior learning (RPL), also called accreditation of prior experiential learning (APEL), may use a portfolio, certificates, interviews or a practical task. The assessor judges evidence against stated learning outcomes; the counsellor explains the process and its limits. Example: Amina, a community health volunteer in Kenya, seeks entry to a diploma. She submits training certificates and a supervisor’s report. The college maps these to two modules and asks for a short written task. She is exempted from one module, not the whole diploma. Rules differ by institution and country, so check current policy.

sections.heading: Study and personal help
sections.text: Guidance also covers study skills: planning time, reading, note making, examination preparation and using library or online resources. A counsellor can help a learner identify a study problem and choose a practical fix, such as a weekly timetable. Personal problems, including money, family pressure, health or harassment, may need counselling or practical referral. The counsellor listens, clarifies options and does not take over the learner’s decisions. Example: Tunde, a night-shift security worker in Lagos, misses classes. With guidance he moves to a weekend group and agrees a study plan.

sections.heading: Ethics and referral
sections.text: Counsellors must work within their competence. They do not diagnose mental illness or give legal or financial advice unless trained and authorised. They refer when a problem exceeds their role. Confidentiality means personal information is not shared without permission. Explain its limits at the start: risk of serious harm or legal duty may require disclosure. Keep records secure and obtain informed consent.

keyPoints: Guidance gives information and advice; counselling explores personal difficulties affecting study.
Recognition of prior learning uses evidence such as portfolios against stated learning outcomes.
Counsellors must not exceed their competence and should refer when needed.
Confidentiality has limits, such as serious risk of harm or legal duty, explained in advance.
Study skills support helps adults plan time, read, take notes and prepare for assessment.
Ethical practice includes informed consent, secure records and the learner’s right to decide.

en.title: Assessment and Evaluation in Adult Education
en.short: Assessing adult learners and evaluating programmes, with portfolios, RPL, Kirkpatrick and CIPP.

sections.heading: Two judgements
sections.text: Assessment judges an individual learner’s progress, achievement or competence. Evaluation judges a programme: its design, teaching, management and results. The two connect, because programme evaluation often uses assessment evidence, but they answer different questions. Assessment asks "How is this learner doing?" Evaluation asks "Is this programme worthwhile, and how can it improve?" Both need evidence and stated criteria.

sections.heading: Formative and summative
sections.text: Formative assessment happens during learning. Its purpose is feedback and improvement, so it is usually not for a final grade. Summative assessment happens at the end and certifies achievement against stated criteria. A tutor may use a short quiz formatively, then a project or portfolio summatively. Adult learners benefit from clear criteria, self-assessment and feedback they can apply at once.

sections.heading: Portfolios and prior learning
sections.text: A portfolio is a structured collection of work, records and reflection that shows what a learner can do. It can serve formative and summative purposes. Recognition of prior learning (RPL) assesses learning gained outside formal courses, such as at work or in community roles, for admission, credit or exemption. RPL needs valid, reliable evidence, explicit standards, fair judgement and respect for confidentiality; it is not simply a claim based on experience.

sections.heading: Evaluating programmes
sections.text: Kirkpatrick’s model has four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour and results. CIPP evaluates context, input, process and product. Use them as planning guides, not rigid formulas. Measure adult outcomes with pre-course and post-course evidence, follow-up after the course, qualitative accounts, and comparison with a suitable group where possible. In a literacy programme with 40 enrolled, 32 finish and 24 improve one level: completion is 32 ÷ 40 = 80%, and outcome gain is 24 ÷ 40 = 60%. Neither figure alone proves the programme caused the gain.

keyPoints: Assessment judges individual learning; evaluation judges a programme’s design, delivery and results.
Formative assessment gives feedback during learning; summative assessment certifies achievement at the end.
Portfolios collect evidence and reflection and can support both formative and summative assessment.
Recognition of prior learning assesses learning gained outside formal courses against explicit standards.
Kirkpatrick’s four levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results; CIPP covers context, input, process and product.
Measure adult outcomes with pre and post evidence and follow-up; completion rate = completers ÷ enrolled × 100%.

en.title: Adult Education Policy and Financing
en.short: How adult education is governed and funded, including cost-sharing, vouchers, fees and equity.

sections.heading: Governance and policy
sections.text: Adult education policy is the set of laws, plans and rules that guide who provides adult learning, what it aims to achieve and how quality is checked. Governance is how these decisions are shared among ministries, agencies, local authorities, providers and qualifications bodies. Legislation is law passed by a parliament or state assembly; it may cover education, skills, literacy or training. A national policy is a government statement of priorities, often with targets and funding commitments. Policies may stand alone or sit inside lifelong learning strategies. They differ by country, so check the current official text.

sections.heading: Who pays
sections.text: Financing is how costs are raised and shared. Government usually funds public programmes from taxes and may grant-aid providers. Employers fund workplace learning, paid study leave and training levies, which are compulsory payments based on payroll. Non-governmental organisations (NGOs), unions, religious bodies and foundations run courses and reach groups that public systems miss, but their funding can be uncertain. Learners pay fees and give time. Cost-sharing means these parties divide the cost. For example, a fictional programme costs 1,000,000 units: government pays 500,000, an employer levy pays 300,000 and learners pay 200,000. With 100 learners, the average fee is 200,000 ÷ 100 = 2,000 units each.

sections.heading: Fees and equity
sections.text: Fees can ration places and exclude poor learners. Equity means fair access and fair chances to succeed, not identical treatment. Governments use subsidies, fee waivers, scholarships, flexible payment and targeted outreach. A voucher is a subsidy that a learner takes to an approved provider. If a course costs 50,000 and the voucher covers 70%, the learner pays 30%, which is 15,000. Vouchers can widen choice, but they need clear information, quality controls and fraud rules, or they may favour learners who know the system. Arrangements vary: some countries have a national adult education law and agency; others rely on education or skills ministries and local government. Rules change, so check current national policy.

keyPoints: Adult education policy is shaped by legislation, national plans and the bodies that govern providers.
Governance is shared among government, agencies, local authorities, providers and qualifications bodies.
Financing comes from public budgets, employer levies, fees, NGOs and learners’ time.
Cost-sharing divides programme costs; in the example, 200,000 ÷ 100 = 2,000 units per learner.
Vouchers are learner-held subsidies and need quality controls and fraud rules to support equity.
Arrangements differ by country and change, so check current national policy and official sources.

en.title: Management and Leadership of Adult Education
en.short: Structures, staffing, budgets, marketing, partnerships, monitoring, and coordinator and facilitator roles.

sections.heading: Structures and roles
sections.text: Management keeps an adult education institution or programme running; leadership sets direction and builds commitment. A simple structure has a governing board, a director or manager, programme coordinators, facilitators, and finance and administrative staff.
