Structures may be centralised, with decisions at the top, or decentralised, with centres deciding locally. The coordinator plans schedules, registers learners, supports facilitators and reports. The facilitator teaches and assesses, and may also recruit learners. Clear job descriptions and lines of accountability prevent confusion.

sections.heading: Staffing and money
sections.text: Staffing means recruiting people with the right subject, adult-learning and administrative skills, then inducting, supervising and developing them. Volunteers need clear roles and support. Budgeting estimates income and expenditure. A line-item budget lists staff, venue, materials, transport and contingency. If a programme expects 40 learners, charges a fee of 2,000 units per learner and receives a grant of 50,000 units, income is (40 × 2,000) + 50,000 = 130,000 units. If costs are 90,000 units, the surplus is 40,000 units. Check figures against real quotations.

sections.heading: Marketing and partners
sections.text: Marketing is not just advertising. It means matching the programme to learners’ needs and making it visible through local languages, community meetings, radio and trusted leaders. Partnerships with employers, libraries, NGOs, local government and community groups can share venues, trainers and referrals. A written agreement should state each partner’s role, costs and how decisions are made. Partnerships fail when expectations are unclear or one partner controls everything.

sections.heading: Monitoring and problems
sections.text: Monitoring tracks attendance, completion, learning outcomes, costs and learner feedback. Quality assurance uses those findings to improve teaching, materials and safety. Common problems in under-resourced settings include late or uncertain funding, few paid staff, high volunteer turnover, poor transport and electricity, weak records, and demands to report numbers rather than learning. Managers should prioritise, keep simple records, share tasks, and review honestly with staff and learners.

keyPoints: Management keeps the programme running; leadership sets direction and builds commitment.
A clear structure names the board, manager, coordinator, facilitator and finance roles.
Staffing covers recruitment, induction, supervision and development, including volunteers.
Budget income = learner fees + grants; surplus = income − expenditure.
Marketing and partnerships should match provision to learner needs and set clear roles.
Monitoring and quality assurance use attendance, completion, outcomes, costs and feedback; under-resourced settings need simple records and prioritisation.

en.title: Ethics and Professionalism in Adult Education
en.short: Ethical issues, professional codes, roles and continuing development for adult educators.

sections.heading: Respect and consent
sections.text: Respect for learners means treating adults as capable people, not children. Use their experience, explain choices, and avoid ridicule. Informed consent means giving clear information about a course or study before the person agrees: its purpose, methods, time, costs, who sees the records, and the right to withdraw. Consent must be voluntary and ongoing, not a signature collected once. A learner may refuse an activity without penalty.

sections.heading: Power and confidentiality
sections.text: Adult educators hold power: they assess, set rules and control access to resources. That power can create dependency or be abused. Set clear boundaries, encourage learners to question and decide, and never exploit a learner financially, sexually or emotionally. Confidentiality means keeping personal information private. It is not absolute: explain its limits, such as a risk of serious harm or a legal duty. Case: Amina, a literacy tutor in Kano, learns that a learner is being harmed at home. She explains the limits, refers the learner to local support under policy, and records only necessary facts.

sections.heading: Indoctrination and codes
sections.text: Indoctrination teaches a belief as unquestionable truth and discourages dissent. Education, by contrast, presents evidence, explains alternatives and invites challenge. An adult educator may hold strong views but should not use the classroom to recruit or silence. Professional codes are written principles adopted by associations or employers. They usually cover competence, honesty, respect, confidentiality and non-discrimination. A code guides judgement; it does not replace it. Check the code that applies in your country and setting.

sections.heading: Roles and growth
sections.text: Adult educators act as facilitators, planners, assessors and representatives of their institution. Each role brings duties: prepare well, assess fairly, keep records safely, and refer learners when needs exceed your competence. Continuing professional development (CPD) is ongoing learning after qualification. It includes reflection, peer observation, reading, workshops and supervision. CPD keeps knowledge current and protects learners from outdated or unsafe practice. Record what you learn and how it changed your work.

keyPoints: Respect learners as adults and obtain voluntary, ongoing informed consent.
Confidentiality has limits; explain them and share information only when necessary.
Power can create dependency, so set boundaries and avoid exploitation.
Education invites challenge; indoctrination suppresses it.
Professional codes guide conduct but require judgement and local rules.
Continuing professional development keeps practice current and accountable.

en.title: Research Methods in Adult Education
en.short: Qualitative and quantitative designs, sampling, instruments, ethics and reporting in adult education research.

sections.heading: Designs and questions
sections.text: Research methods are the planned steps used to answer a question. Quantitative designs measure numbers, test hypotheses and often use surveys or experiments. Qualitative designs explore meaning, experience and context through interviews, focus groups, observation and case studies. Mixed methods combine both. The question should choose the design, not the reverse. For example, a study of why rural women join literacy classes needs qualitative interviews; a study of how many attend needs a survey.

sections.heading: Sampling and instruments
sections.text: Sampling is choosing who takes part. Probability sampling gives everyone a known chance: simple random, stratified or cluster. Non-probability sampling is common in adult education: convenience, purposive, quota and snowball. Purposive sampling selects people who can inform the question. Instruments are the tools: questionnaire, interview guide, focus group guide, observation checklist. Pilot-test instruments, explain terms, and keep questions neutral. In quantitative work check validity and reliability; in qualitative work check credibility and trustworthiness. Example: a researcher wants 40 learners from a programme of 200. A simple random sample can be drawn from a numbered list; 40 ÷ 200 = 20% of learners are selected.

sections.heading: Participatory and action research
sections.text: Participatory research involves participants in defining problems and interpreting findings. Action research is a cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting, repeated as needed. It suits adult education because learners and facilitators can improve practice together. A community literacy group might test a new reading hour, observe attendance, then revise the plan. The researcher must still record evidence and avoid claiming more than the data show.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text: Ethics protect participants and the public. Seek informed consent, explain purpose and risks, keep participation voluntary, protect confidentiality and anonymity, and do no harm. Store data securely. Get approval from the institution’s ethics committee; rules differ by country and institution. A research report usually has title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. State limitations and how the sample affects generalisation.

keyPoints: The research question should determine whether a quantitative, qualitative or mixed design is used.
Probability sampling gives every member a known chance of selection; non-probability sampling is common in adult education.
Instruments such as questionnaires and interview guides must be piloted and worded neutrally.
Action research repeats cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting with participants.
Informed consent, confidentiality, anonymity, voluntary participation and no harm are core ethical requirements.
A research report states methods, findings, limitations and references, and the sampling fraction is sample size ÷ population size.

en.title: Critical Theory and Adult Education
en.short: Freire, Mezirow and Gramsci; critiques of andragogy and human capital theory; power and emancipation.

sections.heading: Critical theory and power
sections.text:
Critical theory, linked to the Frankfurt School (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse, Habermas), asks whose interests knowledge and institutions serve. Habermas named three knowledge interests: technical (control), practical (understanding) and emancipatory (freedom from domination).

Gramsci’s idea of hegemony explains how a dominant group rules by consent, not only by force: schools, media and adult education can spread its worldview as ordinary common sense. Organic intellectuals are thinkers a class produces from within itself. So adult education can either reproduce hegemony or contest it.

sections.heading: Freire and Mezirow
sections.text:
Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968) attacks banking education, where the teacher deposits facts into passive learners. He proposes problem-posing dialogue, in which teacher and learner investigate together. Conscientização is the growth of critical consciousness; praxis is reflection joined to action. He used culture circles in Brazil and later in exile, and said literacy means reading the word and the world.

Mezirow’s transformative learning describes a disorienting dilemma that triggers critical reflection on a frame of reference, then discourse, then changed action. Example: Amina, a trader in Kano, joins a literacy class and learns to keep records. The figures push her to ask why her cooperative never shows its accounts, and she demands them. That is perspective transformation, not just a new skill.

sections.heading: Critiques and debate
sections.text:
Critics say andragogy (Knowles) is a set of assumptions about adult learners, not a tested theory, and that it ignores power, culture and the many adults who feel dependent or anxious. Human capital theory (Schultz, Becker) treats education as investment with measurable returns; critics answer that it ignores learning’s non-economic purposes, blames individuals for structural unemployment, and confuses credentials with skills (the screening hypothesis).

Mezirow is charged with over-individualising change, Freire with romanticising the oppressed. The live question is whether adult education serves adaptation, economic growth or collective emancipation.

keyPoints: Critical theory asks whose interests knowledge and institutions serve.
Habermas named technical, practical and emancipatory knowledge interests.
Gramsci’s hegemony shows dominance working through consent and common sense.
Freire replaces banking education with problem-posing dialogue aimed at conscientização and praxis.
Mezirow’s transformative learning runs from a disorienting dilemma through critical reflection and discourse to changed action.
Andragogy and human capital theory are criticised for ignoring power, structure and non-economic purposes.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and the Master’s Dissertation
en.short: Framing a master’s dissertation: design, theory, mixed methods, ethics, analysis and reporting.

sections.heading: Framing the study
sections.text: A research problem is the gap or puzzle the dissertation addresses, stated precisely enough to guide questions and methods. It is not simply a topic. A master’s study is often framed as one main question with a few sub-questions. The literature review maps what is already known, groups the sources by theme, and shows the gap. It must be critical, not a list of summaries. The theoretical framework is the set of concepts or theory that explains why you expect the relationships you study; it shapes the questions, variables and interpretation.

sections.heading: Design and theory
sections.text: Choose a design that fits the question. Quantitative designs test relationships with numbers; qualitative designs explore meaning and experience; mixed methods combine both. In an explanatory sequential mixed methods design, a survey is analysed first, then interviews explain the survey results. Validity concerns whether the study measures or represents what it claims. In qualitative work, trustworthiness is often judged by credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Reflexivity means examining how your own position, assumptions and choices affect the research.

sections.heading: Proposal and ethics
sections.text: A proposal states the problem, questions, aims, design, sample, instruments, analysis plan, timeline and budget. Ethics approval is normally required before data collection. Requirements vary by country and institution, so check your committee’s current rules. Typical issues are informed consent, confidentiality, anonymity, secure storage, and protection of vulnerable adults. For example, Amina, studying dropout in a Nigerian literacy programme, should explain the study to participants, avoid pressure to join, and keep names out of the data.

sections.heading: Analysis and reporting
sections.text: Analyse data according to the design. Quantitative analysis may use descriptive statistics and then inferential tests; qualitative analysis often uses thematic analysis, coding transcripts and building themes. Mixed methods need integration, not two separate studies. Present the study in a clear order: methods, results, interpretation, limitations and implications. Use tables and quotations sparingly and accurately. State what the study cannot claim. A dissertation defence usually asks you to explain choices and limits, so keep an audit trail, a record of your decisions that shows how you reached your conclusions.

keyPoints: A research problem names a gap, not just a topic.
The literature review must be critical and organised by theme.
The theoretical framework links concepts to questions and interpretation.
Mixed methods combine quantitative and qualitative data, with integration at analysis.
Validity and reflexivity require checking your methods and your own influence.
Ethics approval and a clear analysis and reporting plan are part of the proposal.

en.title: Lifelong Learning Policy and the Future of Adult Education
en.short: It covers lifelong learning policy, UNESCO, OECD and World Bank roles, knowledge economy, inclusion and critiques.

sections.heading: Policy idea
sections.text: Lifelong learning means learning throughout life, in formal, non-formal and informal settings. Non-formal learning is organised learning outside schools and universities, such as adult literacy classes or workplace training. As policy, it is a framework that governments and international bodies use to coordinate education, training and skills across school, work and community. It is wider than adult education, but adult education is a central part. Policy language often speaks of learning from cradle to grave, though the term is used differently by different bodies.

sections.heading: International spread
sections.text: UNESCO promotes lifelong learning as a right and a public good, through adult learning conferences and reports. OECD spreads it through comparative reviews of education and skills, and through work on adult skills. The World Bank links it to human capital, productivity and economic growth, and supports it in education lending. These bodies do not impose one model. Their reports, indicators and funding shape national policy language, especially in low- and middle-income countries.

sections.heading: Economic and social aims
sections.text: Policy often justifies lifelong learning by the knowledge economy, an economy in which growth depends on knowledge, information and technology, so workers must keep learning. Employability means the ability to gain and keep work. Social inclusion means enabling groups such as women, older people, rural dwellers and people with disabilities to take part in learning and society. International statements usually combine these aims: jobs, citizenship and cohesion.

sections.heading: Critiques and variation
sections.text: Critics say policy narrows adult education to economic ends. Human capital theory treats learning as an investment in workers, and employability targets can push civic education, democratic participation and community purposes to the margin, while literacy is often retained but recast as a work skill. Funding may follow measurable skills, while informal and community learning is neglected. Responsibility can shift to individuals who lack time and money. National policies differ: some stress adult literacy, others vocational skills or social inclusion, and funding and governance vary. In a fictional case, a ministry in Kano State funds a skills scheme for market traders but not a women’s literacy circle; the choice shows policy priorities, not a universal model.

keyPoints: Lifelong learning policy is a framework for coordinating learning across formal, non-formal and informal settings throughout life.
UNESCO, OECD and the World Bank spread lifelong learning ideas through reports, comparisons and funding.
Knowledge economy arguments link lifelong learning to skills, productivity and employability.
Social inclusion aims widen access for women, older people, rural dwellers and people with disabilities.
Critics warn that economic targets can crowd out civic, democratic and community purposes.
National policies differ in priorities, funding and governance, so students should check current official documents.
